title: Frailty Assessment
summary: The umbrella guide for the Frailty clinical package: establish baseline vulnerability, identify acute illness and functional decline, and link to focused guides for falls, delirium, CGA and medicines-related harm.

items.title: Must confirm or exclude
mustConfirmOrExclude: The person’s usual cognition, mobility, continence, nutrition, self-care and support before the current illness.
The exact acute change and whether it developed over hours, days or weeks.
Delirium, infection, pain, injury, medication toxicity, dehydration, acute kidney injury, constipation, urinary retention or another reversible precipitant.
Current ability to stand, transfer, walk, toilet, eat, drink and take medicines safely.
Falls, loss of consciousness, prolonged time on the floor or new fear of falling.
Carer availability, home safety, safeguarding concerns and whether essential needs can be met immediately.
The patient’s goals, capacity, treatment escalation plan, advance decisions and preferred place of care.
items.importantLimitation: Do not attribute acute confusion, weakness or immobility to age or frailty without assessing for an acute illness. Frailty scoring during acute illness may overestimate baseline frailty.

items.title: Baseline function and acute change
mustConfirmOrExclude: Usual mobility indoors and outdoors, walking aid, transfer ability and stair use.
Usual personal and instrumental activities of daily living, including washing, dressing, toileting, meals, shopping and medicines.
Usual cognition, communication, mood, sleep and behaviour.
When the change began, how rapidly it progressed and the last known baseline.
What the patient, family or carers identify as the most important new difference.

items.title: Acute illness and reversible causes
mustConfirmOrExclude: Fever, respiratory symptoms, urinary symptoms, abdominal symptoms, wounds or other infection features.
Pain, recent fall, head injury or occult trauma.
Reduced intake, vomiting, diarrhoea, constipation, urinary retention or incontinence change.
Breathlessness, oedema, chest symptoms, dizziness, syncope or focal neurological symptoms.
Recent blood results, including renal function, glucose and inflammatory markers where available.

items.title: Delirium and cognition
mustConfirmOrExclude: Recent change or fluctuation in concentration, responses, orientation or memory.
New hallucinations, agitation, sleep reversal, withdrawal or reduced interaction.
Hypoactive features such as unusual quietness, slow responses, reduced movement or poor appetite.
Known dementia, cognitive impairment, learning disability or previous delirium.
Collateral account from someone who knows the patient’s normal behaviour.

items.title: Falls, mobility and fear of falling
mustConfirmOrExclude: Any fall in the previous year, including frequency, circumstances and injury.
Loss of consciousness, presyncope, dizziness or inability to get up independently.
Time spent on the floor and possible pressure, dehydration or muscle injury consequences.
New gait change, weakness, pain or reduced confidence.
Walking aids, footwear, home hazards and whether usual equipment is available and used.

items.title: Nutrition, hydration and continence
mustConfirmOrExclude: Weight loss, reduced appetite, swallowing difficulty, dentition or inability to prepare meals.
Usual and current fluid intake and access to drinks.
Vomiting, diarrhoea, high-output stoma or other losses.
Urinary frequency, retention, new incontinence, constipation or faecal impaction.
Who provides food, fluids and toileting support and whether this remains reliable.

items.title: Medicines and treatment burden
mustConfirmOrExclude: Full medicines reconciliation, adherence and recent changes.
Sedatives, psychotropics, opioids, anticholinergics, antihypertensives, diuretics, glucose-lowering medicines and anticoagulants.
Adverse effects including falls, postural hypotension, constipation, confusion, bleeding or acute kidney injury.
Whether the person can organise and take medicines correctly.
Treatments or appointments that create disproportionate burden or conflict with current goals.

items.title: Support, safeguarding and goals of care
mustConfirmOrExclude: Living arrangement, formal care package, family support and overnight availability.
Carer strain, breakdown, missed visits or inability to meet essential needs.
Home heating, food, fluids, phone access, mobility equipment and environmental hazards.
Safeguarding concerns, neglect, coercion or unexplained injuries.
Capacity for the current decision and any lasting power of attorney or nominated decision-maker.
Advance care plan, treatment escalation plan, resuscitation decision and preferred place of care.

items.title: New delirium
urgentFeatures: Acute or fluctuating confusion, inattention, hallucinations, agitation or altered consciousness.
Hypoactive change with unusual withdrawal, slow responses, reduced mobility or poor intake.
A positive 4AT or strong collateral concern about acute cognitive change.
implications: Identify and manage the underlying cause or combination of causes; delirium is a medical syndrome, not a normal consequence of frailty.

items.title: Rapid functional decline
urgentFeatures: New inability to stand, transfer, walk, toilet, eat, drink or take essential medicines.
Rapid decline over hours or days without an established benign explanation.
Unsafe return to the current environment.
implications: Requires acute medical assessment and a function-led disposition plan, even when observations are not markedly abnormal.

items.title: Fall, injury or prolonged lie
urgentFeatures: Head injury, anticoagulant use, focal pain, deformity or inability to weight-bear.
Loss of consciousness or unexplained fall.
Unable to get up independently or prolonged time on the floor.
New neurological deficit or persistent severe pain.
implications: Use the appropriate head-injury, trauma, syncope or falls pathway and assess complications of the prolonged lie.

items.title: Unmet essential care needs
urgentFeatures: No reliable access to food, fluids, medicines, toileting, repositioning or urgent help.
Pressure injury, severe self-neglect or repeated missed care.
implications: A medically stable patient may still require urgent admission, crisis care or safeguarding action when essential needs cannot be met.

items.title: Safeguarding concern
urgentFeatures: Unexplained injuries, fearfulness, coercion, neglect, financial exploitation or inconsistent accounts.
Concern that a dependent adult is being left without essential care.
Immediate danger in the current environment.
implications: Follow the local adult-safeguarding pathway and document the concern, capacity, immediate protection plan and people informed.

items.title: Possible end-of-life deterioration
urgentFeatures: Progressive decline with reduced intake, increasing sleep, worsening function and advanced life-limiting illness.
Symptoms not controlled by the current anticipatory plan.
Uncertainty about whether an acute reversible cause should be treated or whether transfer matches the patient’s goals.
implications: Clarify goals, capacity, advance plans and senior clinical responsibility; arrange urgent palliative or medical support rather than assuming deterioration is inevitable.

items.title: General assessment and observations
howToTest: Assess appearance, distress, interaction and evidence of acute illness.
Record temperature, heart rate, blood pressure, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation and early warning score.
Review trends and compare with known baseline.
Assess pain using a method the person can understand.
normal: Physiologically stable, comfortable and interacting at baseline.
abnormal: Abnormal physiology, pain, altered consciousness or reduced engagement.
A normal early warning score with substantial new functional decline.
implications: Physiology should be interpreted alongside function and collateral history; older people may have serious illness without fever or marked tachycardia.

items.title: Delirium assessment
howToTest: Ask a collateral source about acute change or fluctuation.
Assess alertness, attention, orientation and acute change using the 4AT when competent to do so.
Look specifically for hypoactive delirium.
Identify possible causes including infection, pain, retention, constipation, hypoxia, metabolic disturbance and medicines.
normal: No acute or fluctuating cognitive or behavioural change and 4AT does not indicate delirium.
abnormal: Acute change, fluctuation, inattention, altered alertness or a 4AT indicating possible delirium.
implications: A competent practitioner should use the 4AT when delirium indicators are present; the final diagnosis requires appropriate clinical expertise.
items.importantLimitation: A known dementia diagnosis does not explain a sudden change. When delirium and dementia are difficult to distinguish, manage delirium first.

items.title: Mobility, transfers and gait
howToTest: Observe bed or chair mobility, sit-to-stand, transfers and walking using the usual aid where safe.
Assess balance, lower-limb strength, pain and confidence.
Compare with usual mobility from collateral history.
Do not force performance testing in an acutely unwell person.
normal: Function is close to baseline and mobility is safe with usual support.
abnormal: New assistance requirement, inability to stand, unsafe gait, focal weakness or marked deconditioning.
implications: New mobility loss changes disposition and requires assessment for acute illness, injury and rehabilitation needs.

items.title: Baseline frailty and vulnerability
howToTest: Describe baseline independence, mobility, cognition and support before the acute illness.
Use a locally approved validated frailty tool where required.
Base any frailty score on the usual pre-illness state rather than the current acute deterioration.
Document the source of collateral information and uncertainty.
normal: Independent baseline with preserved reserve and little assistance.
abnormal: Dependence in daily activities, reduced mobility, cognitive impairment, recurrent falls or high treatment burden.
implications: Frailty should prompt comprehensive, proportionate care planning but must not be used alone to limit treatment.
items.importantLimitation: NICE advises caution when assessing frailty during acute illness and advises against physical performance tools in an acutely unwell person.

items.title: Falls-focused examination
howToTest: Assess injuries, footwear, feet, vision, hearing and neurological status.
Measure lying and standing blood pressure when safe.
Assess gait, balance, mobility and muscle strength.
Review medicines and environmental hazards.
Assess whether the person can get up or summon help after a fall.
normal: No injury, unexplained loss of consciousness or new gait and balance impairment.
abnormal: Injury, recurrent falls, postural hypotension, unsafe gait, visual or sensory impairment or inability to get up.
implications: People living with frailty who have fallen generally require comprehensive falls assessment and tailored management.

items.title: Nutrition and hydration
howToTest: Review weight trend, appetite, intake, swallowing, dentition and ability to feed independently.
Assess hydration, urine output and ongoing losses.
Observe a drink or meal only when safe and clinically appropriate.
Identify who provides meals and fluids.
normal: Weight, intake and swallowing are stable and support is adequate.
abnormal: Weight loss, poor intake, dysphagia, dehydration, acute kidney injury or inability to access food and fluids.
implications: Nutritional or fluid deficits may cause delirium and functional decline and will recur unless the practical cause is corrected.

items.title: Medication and postural assessment
howToTest: Reconcile all medicines and recent changes.
Assess for sedation, anticholinergic effects, constipation, bleeding, hypoglycaemia and renal accumulation.
Measure lying and standing blood pressure when symptoms or falls suggest postural hypotension.
Confirm how medicines are organised and administered.
normal: Medicines are appropriate, correctly taken and not causing obvious harm.
abnormal: Sedation, hypotension, falls, confusion, hypoglycaemia, bleeding, constipation or acute kidney injury linked to treatment.
implications: Structured medication review may identify modifiable causes of deterioration and treatment burden.

items.title: Skin, continence and personal care
howToTest: Inspect pressure areas, wounds, bruising and skin infection where consent and circumstances allow.
Assess continence change, retention, constipation and toileting ability.
Assess hygiene, clothing and evidence that personal care needs are being met.
normal: Skin intact, continence needs managed and personal care adequate.
abnormal: Pressure injury, wounds, unexplained bruising, retention, impaction or unmet hygiene and toileting needs.
implications: May identify infection, pain, neglect, immobility complications or the need for increased care support.

items.title: Environment and support
howToTest: Confirm who is present, when carers next attend and how urgent help is obtained.
Assess immediate access to food, fluids, heating, lighting, phone, toilet and mobility equipment.
Identify hazards, stairs and whether the person can enter or leave the property safely.
Confirm the receiving service has accepted responsibility before leaving.
normal: Essential needs can be met reliably and the environment supports the agreed plan.
abnormal: Carer breakdown, absent essential supplies, unsafe environment, no emergency access or unclear clinical responsibility.
implications: Social and environmental failure can make home management unsafe even when the medical condition appears stable.

items.title: Stable frailty without acute deterioration
commonFindings: Function, cognition, intake and mobility are at usual baseline.
No new symptoms, injury, delirium or physiological deterioration.
Current care package and medicines remain workable.
implications: Address preventive care, falls risk, treatment burden and advance planning through routine or proactive services rather than an acute pathway.

items.title: Acute illness superimposed on frailty
commonFindings: New functional or cognitive decline with symptoms or signs of infection, pain, metabolic disturbance or organ dysfunction.
The presenting complaint may be nonspecific, such as weakness, a fall or reduced intake.
Reduced physiological reserve increases the risk of rapid deterioration.
implications: Treat and monitor the acute diagnosis while preserving mobility, cognition, nutrition and the patient’s goals of care.

items.title: Delirium
commonFindings: Acute onset or fluctuation over hours or days.
Inattention, altered alertness, hallucinations, agitation or hypoactive withdrawal.
Collateral history confirms a change from baseline.
implications: Identify and treat the underlying cause, provide reorientation and involve family or carers.

items.title: Deconditioning after illness or inactivity
commonFindings: Reduced strength, endurance and confidence after bed rest, hospital admission or illness.
No focal neurological deficit or acute injury explaining the whole decline.
Function improves with assistance but remains below baseline.
implications: Requires rehabilitation, graded activity and support planning while continuing to exclude active medical causes.

items.title: Medication-related deterioration
commonFindings: Temporal relationship to a new medicine, dose change or accumulation during renal impairment.
Sedation, postural hypotension, falls, constipation, confusion, bleeding or hypoglycaemia.
Complex regimen or administration errors.
implications: Arrange structured medication review and document changes, monitoring and responsibility for follow-up.

items.title: Frailty with recurrent falls
commonFindings: Fall in the previous year with frailty, injury, loss of consciousness, inability to get up or two or more falls.
Gait, balance, postural blood pressure, medicines, vision or environmental risks may contribute.
implications: Offer or refer for comprehensive falls assessment and tailored management.

preferredImaging: Imaging directed by the suspected injury or acute diagnosis.
keyTriggers: Head injury, focal bony pain, deformity, inability to weight-bear or new neurological deficit.
guidance: Do not image frailty itself. Use the relevant head-injury or trauma pathway when clinical features indicate injury.

items.title: Malnutrition or fluid deficit contributing to decline
commonFindings: Weight loss, reduced intake, swallowing or dental problems, dehydration or acute kidney injury.
Reduced strength, delirium or falls.
Practical barriers or inadequate support.
implications: Treat metabolic complications and correct the food, fluid, swallowing and support problem that caused the deficit.

items.title: Carer breakdown or social crisis
commonFindings: Medical condition may be stable but essential care cannot be delivered.
Exhausted or unavailable carers, missed visits, unsafe housing or absent equipment.
Patient cannot manage food, fluids, toileting, medicines or emergency access independently.
implications: Requires urgent coordinated health and social-care planning; admission may be necessary when essential needs cannot be met safely.

items.title: Advanced frailty and possible end-of-life decline
commonFindings: Progressive loss of function, reduced intake and increased sleep in advanced irreversible illness.
Existing advance plan or preference to remain at home.
Potential reversible causes and symptom burden have been considered.
implications: Provide proportionate treatment aligned with the patient’s goals and ensure anticipatory medication, carer support and out-of-hours responsibility are explicit.
items.importantLimitation: Frailty or age alone must not be used to assume that an acute condition is untreatable or that hospital care is inappropriate.

items.title: Potentially suitable for supported home management
commonFindings: Acute diagnosis is identified, stable and manageable in the available service.
Cognition and function are at baseline or can be safely supported.
Food, fluids, medicines, toileting and mobility needs can be met immediately.
A named clinician or team has accepted follow-up responsibility.
The patient’s capacity, preferences and escalation plan are documented.
implications: Home management is a coordinated care plan, not simply the absence of a hospital indication.

items.title: Frailty and functional deterioration
safetyNetting: Any significant deterioration in breathing, chest pain or collapse – call 999.

Seek urgent reassessment for new or worsening confusion; inability to stand, walk, eat, drink, pass urine or take essential medicines; a further fall or injury; fever or rigors; uncontrolled pain; marked drowsiness; or any situation in which essential care can no longer be provided safely.
Follow the agreed review plan and contact the named service if function, intake or cognition has not returned towards baseline within the expected timeframe.
items.importantLimitation: Safety-netting is ineffective unless the person or carer can recognise deterioration, contact the service and obtain a timely response.
